_comment: Steps shared by open arterial operations (ruptured AAA repair, femoral embolectomy, and future bypass and trauma repairs). Authored once, referenced by many. Procedure-only steps stay in each procedure's steps_local.

step.vasc.vessel-control.title: Proximal and distal control before opening the artery
step.vasc.vessel-control.why: An artery opened without control bleeds at arterial pressure into a field you can no longer see. Control first turns a haemorrhage into a planned arteriotomy.
how: Expose the artery above and below the planned arteriotomy, in healthy tissue away from haematoma or disease where possible.
Pass slings or tapes around each vessel, including the important branches, and identify where each clamp will go before applying any.
Handle the artery by its adventitia or slings, never with forceps on the intima-bearing wall.
State aloud to the anaesthetist when a clamp is going on and when it is coming off.
structuresAtRisk: Accompanying veins, which tear easily during circumferential dissection
Small side branches avulsed by traction on slings
pitfalls: Clamping a heavily calcified segment, which cracks the plaque and causes a dissection.
Dissecting circumferentially around a vessel when a clamp applied from the front would do.

step.vasc.heparin.title: Systemic heparin before clamping
step.vasc.heparin.why: Static blood beyond a clamp clots within minutes. Heparin before clamping prevents distal thrombosis that would undo the repair.
how: Agree the heparin dose with the anaesthetist per local protocol, and give it a few minutes before the clamps go on.
Record the time and dose; check clotting (for example ACT) during long clamp times if the unit uses it.
In active haemorrhage, such as a ruptured aneurysm or trauma, the dose may be reduced or omitted: decide this explicitly and say so.
pitfalls: Clamping before the heparin has circulated.
Forgetting that the patient is heparinised when assessing bleeding at closure.

step.vasc.flush-backbleed.title: Flushing and back-bleeding before the final sutures
step.vasc.flush-backbleed.why: Clot, air and debris left in the lumen go straight to the distal bed when flow is restored. Forward flushing and back-bleeding clear them while you still have control.
how: Before tying the last suture, release the distal clamp briefly to back-bleed, then the proximal clamp to forward-flush.
Irrigate the lumen with heparinised saline and remove any loose thrombus or intimal flaps.
Assess the strength of back-bleeding: weak or absent back-bleeding suggests residual distal thrombus.
pitfalls: Skipping the flush to save a minute at the end of a long operation.
Accepting poor back-bleeding without imaging or further catheter passes.

step.vasc.restore-flow.title: Restoring flow with the anaesthetist warned
step.vasc.restore-flow.why: Declamping releases cold, acidic, potassium-rich blood into the circulation and drops the pressure suddenly. Warned and staged, it is uneventful; unannounced, it can arrest the patient.
how: Tell the anaesthetist before releasing each clamp so that volume and vasopressors are ready.
Release slowly, one limb or one clamp at a time, and be ready to reapply if the pressure falls sharply.
Check the suture lines for bleeding as pressure returns, and repair with fine sutures while still able to clamp.
pitfalls: Releasing both iliac clamps together after a long clamp time.
Chasing suture line bleeding with more sutures before giving heparin reversal, warmth and clotting factors a chance.

step.vasc.perfusion-check.title: Confirming distal perfusion before leaving theatre
step.vasc.perfusion-check.why: A technically perfect anastomosis with a thrombosed or embolised distal bed is a failed operation. The time to find it is while the patient is still on the table.
how: Examine both feet (or hands) under the drapes: colour, capillary refill, palpable pulses, and handheld Doppler signals.
Perform completion angiography or duplex when the result is in doubt, or routinely after embolectomy.
Compare with the pre-operative state and the other limb, and document what you found.
pitfalls: Draping the feet out of view, so that distal ischaemia is found in recovery.
Assuming a poor foot is vasospasm and closing.
